Question: Irrigant that is least associated with allergic reactions in endodontics
Explanation:
NAOCL:
• Hypersensitivity and contact dermatitis may occur in rare situations.
• When hypersensitivity to NaOCl is suspected or confirmed, chlorhexidine should not be used either because of its chlorine content. CHX:

Although iodine is not generally considered an allergen, some patients are hypersensitive to this compound and may be considered to have an iodine “allergy.”

Question: During lateral condensation technique, spreader should be turned to __ degree before removal?
Explanation: A spreader is pre-fitted in the canal allowing its insertion to within 1.0-2.0 mm from the working length. Auxiliary cones are also selected to closely match the size of the spreader. After introducing a small amount of sealer in the prepared root canal, the master cone Is slowly inserted to the working length. The spreader is then introduced between the master cone and the dentin walls to make room for the first auxiliary cone. The spreader is slowly removed laterally (and somewhat vertically) compacted, rotating the instrument in 180-degree motions. During this movement the gutta-percha is compacted against a canal wall while, at the same time, space is created laterally to the master cone for the auxiliary cones. The spreader is then removed by rotating it back and forth as it is withdrawn from the canal and an auxiliary cone is inserted in the empty space.

Question: To treat hot tooth, which of the following is not indicated?
Explanation:
Obtaining anesthesia is often difficult in patients with endodontic pain. One of the explanations has been that conventional anesthetic techniques do not provide profound pulpal anesthesia, and patients with preexisting hyperalgesia may be unable to tolerate any noxious input. Another explanation relates to the theory that inflamed tissue has a lower pH, which reduces the amount of the base form of anesthetic that penetrates the nerve membrane. Another explanation for failure is that nerves arising from inflamed tissue have altered resting potentials and decreased excitability thresholds. Another factor might be the Nav-R sodium channels, which are resistant to the action of local anesthetics, are increased in inflamed dental pulp, and are sensitized by prostaglandins. Finally, patients in pain are often apprehensive, which lowers the pain threshold.

Therefore, practitioners should use supplemental techniques (e.g., intraosseous or intraligamentary injections if an IAN block fails to provide pulp anesthesia) for patients with irreversible pulpitis. Premedication with NSAIDs can also increase anesthetic efficacy in such conditions.

Question: What is the treatment of the following condition present in the image?
Option A: Physiological splint of 4 weeks + RCT of coronal + Apical third is removed
Option B: Physiological splint of 4 weeks+ Apexification of coronal segment
Explanation:
The X-ray shows mid root fracture with line of fracture. Here there will be a coronal and apical segment. The coronal segment should be reduced quickly and a functional (nonrigid) splint is placed for 4 weeks.

In most cases, permanent necrosis occurs in the coronal segment, with only the apical segment remaining vital. Therefore, endodontic treatment is indicated in the coronal root segment unless periapical pathology is seen in the apical segment.

In most cases the pulpal lumen is wide at the apical extent of the coronal segment, and long-term calcium hydroxide treatment or an MTA apical plug is required after a hard tissue barrier has formed apically in the coronal segment and periradicular healing has taken place.

Situation in which both apical segment and coronal segment become necrosed:
When both the coronal and apical pulp are necrotic, treatment is more complicated. Medicaments, and filling materials all have a detrimental effect on healing of the fracture site.
• In more apical root fractures, necrotic apical segments can be surgically removed.
• Retrograde MTA apical plug is indicated in the coronal segment.
• Endo implant can also be considered if the length is less.

Sequence of treatment:
- Splint - Initiate RCT - Surgical removal of apical segment - retrograde MTA (or)
- Splint - RCT - Obturation- Endo Implant

Question: After reimplantation which of the following type of resorption occurs most commonly?
Explanation:
After reimplantation, the tooth can undergo internal root resorption, external inflammatory root resorption or replacement root resorption. But the most common is the external inflammatory root resorption.

External Inflammatory Root resorption:
• Infection is the cause for this resorption. Avulsion represents a combined injury to the pulp and PDL, in which microorganisms, primarily located in the pulp spaces and in the dentinal tubules, trigger external inflammatory resorption, root surface and adjacent alveolar bone.
• It can affect all parts of the root and is typically diagnosed 2-4 weeks after injury. The resorption is a rapidly progressing process that may result in total resorption of the root within a few months. It is almost exclusively related to acute trauma and is especially common after intrusion injuries and replantation of avulsed teeth.
• Replantation of avulsed, full root needs to include treatment of the pulp to prevent infection-related resorption.

Note:
• Most common type of resorption in intrusive, extrusive luxation and luxation injuries- External inflammatory resorption
• External replacement resorption is seen commonly with delayed replantation of avulsed teeth.

Question: Tenderness on percussion in due to
Explanation:
The percussion test is a simple means of assessing whether there is inflammation or other changes occurring in the periradicular tissues.
• Normal — the same feeling as that patient’s other teeth, and with no tenderness or pain; this typically indicates clinically normal periradicular tissues.
• Tender — a painful response when percussing the tooth; this typically indicates acute apical periodontitis or acute apical abscess.
• Different sensation — the patient reports that the tooth feels “different” on percussion compared to how the adjacent teeth felt—it is not painful or tender; this typically indicates chronic apical periodontitis or a chronic apical abscess.
• Ankylosis sound — there is no pain but percussion produces a dull sound that is different from that produced when percussing the adjacent teeth. This indicates the tooth has ankylosis.

Question: Which of the following irrigants help in differentiating between irreversible & reversible pulpitis and decides which tooth will go for pulpotomy or RCT?
Explanation: The irrigant which decides which tooth will go for pulpotomy or RCT is 5% sodium hypochlorite. After pulp is exposed in pulp capping/ partial pulpotomy/ pulpotomy, the bleeding from that exposure should be stopped after application of cotton pellet with hypochlorite in 5-10 min. The bleach causes chemical amputation of the blood coagulum, removes damaged pulp cells, dentin chips, and other debris, and provides hemorrhage control with minimal damage to the “normal” pulp tissue underneath. If the bleeding does not control in 10 min, then it is irreversible inflammation of pulp which requires deep excavation, and the clinical diagnosis of pulp will change accordingly.

Explanation:
Restorative Diagnosis: Pulpal Exposures and Hemorrhage:
It has been reported that the size of the exposure, the appearance of the pulp, and the color and amount of hemorrhage are important factors in diagnosing the extent of inflammation in a pulp exposed by caries. In accidental pulpal exposures, the bleeding point should be identified. If the patient has pain, anesthesia should be given. Eugenol has an obtundant effect on exposed pulp, so it can be used if it is available. But recognition of the bleeding site is important, and the bleeding should be controlled. The bleeding from that exposure should be stopped after application of cotton pellet with hypochlorite in 5-10 min. If the bleeding does not control in 10 min, then it is due to irreversible inflammation of pulp which requires deep excavation.

Question: A 9-year-old child with history of trauma reported to your clinic. Radiograph of avulsed tooth replanted with 1 year back is given below. Which of the following is correct?
Option C: B. pulp canal obliteration; i. good prognosis
Option D: B. pulp canal obliteration; ii. Bad prognosis
Explanation:
Replanted teeth should be monitored clinically and radiographically at 2 weeks (when the splint is removed), 4 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, one year, and yearly thereafter for at least five years. Clinical and radiographic examination will provide information to determine the outcome. Two types of resorptions may occur concurrently- inflammatory and replacement resorption. Both of them indicate poor outcome.

Pulp canal obliteration might occur in few open apex cases. Pulp canal obliteration is common after luxation injuries. It can usually be diagnosed within the first year after injury and was found to be more frequent in teeth with open apices (>0.7 mm radiographically), in teeth with extrusive and lateral luxation injuries, and in teeth that have been rigidly splinted.

Favorable outcomes

a) Closed apex:
Asymptomatic, functional, normal mobility, no sensitivity to percussion, and normal percussion sound. No radiolucencies and no radiographic evidence of root resorption. The lamina dura appears normal.

b) Open apex:
Asymptomatic, functional, normal mobility, no sensitivity to percussion, and normal percussion sound. Radiographic evidence of continued root formation and tooth eruption. Pulp canal obliteration is expected and can be recognized radiographically sometime during the first year after the trauma. It is considered to be the mechanism by which the “pulp” heals after replantation of avulsed immature permanent teeth.

Question: Which of the following will not cause external inflammatory root resorption?
Explanation:
Etiology and Pathogenesis of External Inflammatory Resorption (EIR):
• A specific set of conditions is required for the initiation and progression of EIR. Under normal conditions, permanent teeth are resistant to resorption. Odontoclasts do not adhere to the nonmineralized layers covering the external root surface and the root canal wall (i.e., the precementum and predentin, respectively). For EIR to occur, the precementum should be damaged during traumatic dental injuries (e.g., intrusion, lateral luxation, and avulsion), pressure on the root surface during orthodontic treatment and from impacted teeth, cysts, and tumors may also denude the protective precementum from the root surface and therefore initiate external root resorption.
• Microbes and/or their toxins located in the root canal and the dentinal tubules, diffuse through the tubules and directly stimulate the resorbing osteoclasts. The resorption process intensifies and accelerates. The resorbed mineralized tissue is replaced by granulation tissue, which ultimately invades the pulp space if the process continues.

Explanation:
In lateral luxation reposition the tooth digitally by disengaging it from its locked position and gently reposition it into its original location under local anesthesia. Stabilize the tooth for 4 weeks using a passive and flexible splint.

Stabilization/Splinting: Type and Duration
• Current evidence supports short-term, passive, and flexible splints for splinting of luxated, avulsed, and root-fractured teeth. In the case of alveolar bone fractures, splinting of the teeth may be used for bone segment immobilization.
• Splinting is considered best practice in order to maintain the repositioned tooth in its correct position and to favor initial healing while providing comfort and controlled function.
• Use of antibiotics: There is limited evidence for the use of systemic antibiotics in the emergency management of luxation injuries and no evidence that antibiotics improve the outcomes for root-fractured teeth. Antibiotic use remains at the discretion of the clinician as infections are often accompanied by soft tissue and other associated injuries, which may require other surgical intervention. In addition, the patient’s medical status may warrant antibiotic coverage.

Note: Replantation of avulsed tooth requires antibiotic coverage.

Question: Regenerative endodontic procedures are all except?
Explanation:
Regenerative endodontic procedures (REPs) have been defined as biologically based procedures designed to replace damaged structures such as dentin, root structures, and cells of the pulp-dentin complex. This new treatment modality has emerged as an alternative that, in addition to healing apical periodontitis, aims to promote normal pulpal physiologic functions.
• These include continued root development, immune competency, and normal nociception, as seen in some published cases. Thus, the ultimate goal of these procedures is to regenerate the components and normal function of the pulp-dentin complex.
• Revascularization of immature apex, Pulp reimplantation and Postnatal stem cell therapy are some of the REP’s.

Question: In bone defect after periapical surgery, how much time it will take for bone deposition?
Explanation: About 3 to 4 weeks after surgery, an excisional osseous wound is 75% to 80% filled with trabeculae surrounded by intensely active osteoid and osteoblastic cells. A reforming periosteum can be seen on the outer surface of the wound. It is highly cellular and has more fibrous connective tissue oriented parallel to the plane of the former cortical plate. At 8 weeks after surgery, the trabeculae are larger and denser and the osteoblasts less active; these cells occupy about 80% of the original wound. Also, fewer osteoid cells are associated with the maturing trabeculae. The overlying periosteum has reformed and is in contact with the newly developed bone. The osseous defect typically is filled with bone tissue by 16 weeks after surgery, but the cortical plate has not yet totally.

Question: Which of the following property of NaOCl is least desirable for pulpotomy procedure?
Explanation:
Sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) has been successfully used for many years in endodontic therapy as an irrigant for permanent teeth. At low concentrations it has been found to be biocompatible, non-irritating, and hemostatic to exposed pulpal tissue. It can eliminate bacteria, superficial inflamed tissue, and dentine debris from exposure sites, while leaving the deeper healthy pulp tissue unharmed.

The technique of NaOCl pulpotomy includes removal of the coronal pulp, achieving hemostasis, placing a cotton pellet saturated with 3% NaOCl for 30 seconds, rinsing with sterile saline and filling the pulp chamber with ZOE. The success rate for this treatment is similar to that of formocresol.

The third study concluded that the use of sodium hypochlorite, as an antimicrobial agent, prior to application of the pulpotomy dressing, improved the success rate of calcium hydroxide pulpotomies, to equal the success of MTA pulpotomies for observation periods of up to 12 months.

So, options ‘A’, ‘C’, and ‘D’ are the desired properties of NaOCl to be used as pulpotomy agent. Option B will lead to internal resorption. So, it is not the desirable property.

Question: On a radiograph, it was seen that GP was tightly compacted on the coronal third but loosely spaced on apical region. The reason is?
Option B: Inadequate length of the spreader inserted short of apex
Explanation:
The lateral condensation technique has several drawbacks:
• Being a “cold” technique, the gutta-percha cones don’t form a homogeneous, compact mass.
• Filling of lateral portals of exit occurs less frequently than when vertical compaction is performed and is always constituted of sealer, not gutta-percha.
• The spreader should be placed within 1 mm to 2 mm of the working length. If not carefully done, it may exert excessive lateral forces, increasing the risk of root fracture. Also, if spreader not inserted of adequate length, it results in voids and less density of GP.
• When considering that heat is not used, the most apical portion of the master cone does not undergo significant modification. The seal in this area is, therefore, mainly entrusted to the sealer.

Question: Patient is suffering from pain at night since a month. One portion of gingiva is completely recessed in between two teeth. Last night she had severe cold sensitivity which persisted for one hour. What will be the diagnosis?
Explanation:
The clinical scenario is a case of irreversible pulpitis.

Characteristics of irreversible pulpitis:
• Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis exhibits pain usually caused by a hot or cold stimulus, or pain that occurs spontaneously. The pain persists for several minutes to hours, lingering after removal of the thermal stimulus.
• Spontaneous pain may come and go without an apparent cause. It may be intermittent or continuous.
• The patient may describe the pain as sharp, piercing, or shooting, and it is generally severe.
• The patient may also complain of postural pain, i.e., change of position (bending over or lying down) exacerbates the pain. This is due to the increase in intrapulpal pressure when the patient changes position from a standing posture to a supine (lying down) posture.
• The patient may also have pain referred to adjacent teeth, to the temple or sinuses when an upper posterior tooth is involved, or to the ear when a lower posterior tooth is affected.
• In later stages, the pain is more severe and is generally described as boring, gnawing, or throbbing, or as if the tooth was under constant pressure.
• Patients are often kept awake at night by the pain (nocturnal pain), which continues to be intolerable despite all their efforts at analgesia. Pain is increased by heat and is sometimes relieved by cold, although continued cold may intensify the pain.

Question: Which of the following techniques will lead to least dentinal crack while biomechanical preparation:
Option B: Crown down with hand Stainless steel Files
Option C: Crown down with rotary NiTi files
Option D: Crown down with Hand K files
Explanation:
Microcracks Caused by root canal instrumentation: (various studies):
• According to Dilek et al, all instruments, including hand instruments, cause dentinal defects. When rotary files are used, the latter are magnified in comparison to hand files.
• Hand K and H stainless steel files produced less number of defects than rotary NiTi file.
• Root canal preparation using nickel-titanium rotary and reciprocating files often results in microcracks in the remaining radicular dentin.
• Rotary files induce strain on the dentin, as measured in the surface layers of the root dentin, which likely exceeds the elasticity of the dentin, causing subsequent microcracks.
• Additional stress, by either root obturation with lateral compaction or by retreatment that was applied to roots that were previously instrumented with rotary files, caused some of the microcracks to propagate and become through-and-through fractures that were indistinguishable from VRF.
